cards.design_implication: A research design aiming to replicate or extend this population analysis should utilize a catalog with explicit classification of binary components into BBH, BNS, and NSBH categories.
cards.evidence_excerpt: We report on the population properties of 76 compact binary mergers detected with gravitational waves below a false alarm rate of 1 per year through the cumulative Gravitational Wave Transient Catalog 3 (GWTC-3). The catalog contains three classes of binary mergers: binary black hole (BBH), binary neutron star (BNS), and neutron star–black hole (NSBH) mergers.
limitations: The count of 76 events is specific to the GWTC-3 catalog with a False Alarm Rate threshold of < 1 yr^-1.
This statement describes the data source and classification scheme, not the statistical inference method itself.
cards.statement: The study infers population properties of 76 compact binary mergers from the GWTC-3 catalog, categorizing them into binary black hole (BBH), binary neutron star (BNS), and neutron star–black hole (NSBH) classes.

cards.design_implication: A study design prioritizing BBH sample size over strict event purity may justify using a higher FAR threshold (e.g., < 1 yr^-1) compared to analyses requiring mixed population purity.
does_not_establish: The exact statistical model used to estimate the proportion of non-astrophysical events.
The performance of this threshold on non-BBH populations.
cards.evidence_excerpt: Considering the BBH population only, as in Section V, we lower the detection threshold to count events with FAR $\mathrm { o f < 1 y r ^ { - 1 } }$ , resulting in 69 confident BBH events.
limitations: The excerpt mentions 'confident' BBH events, but the text elsewhere notes that at this threshold, approximately 4.6 events are expected to be non-astrophysical.
The specific threshold of < 1 yr^-1 is tied to the BBH-only analysis context.
cards.statement: For analyses focused solely on the Binary Black Hole (BBH) population, the detection threshold is relaxed to a False Alarm Rate (FAR) of < 1 yr^-1 to increase sample size, accepting that this may include less significant events.
